subsystems.name: Feedstock module
subsystems.role: stores and meters the simple molecules the device actually builds from — refined sugars, amino acids, methanol, salts — not raw elements.

subsystems.name: Reaction core
subsystems.role: where bonds are made. Realistic designs use immobilised enzyme cascades or engineered microbes, since chemistry proceeds by reactions between prepared molecules rather than by assembling atoms from elements.

subsystems.name: Separation and purification
subsystems.role: isolates the wanted molecule from the reaction mixture.

subsystems.name: Sensing and control
subsystems.role: watches the reaction and adjusts it in real time.

subsystems.name: Forming and dispensing
subsystems.role: turns the purified product into something usable — a textured food portion or a sterile dose.

subsystems.name: Waste and containment
subsystems.role: handles solvents, spent catalyst and any engineered organisms safely in a home.

buildSteps.title: Pick the target molecule
buildSteps.detail: Every synthesis begins by defining the exact product and a route to it — the set of reactions that can build it from available feedstock.

buildSteps.title: Engineer the catalysts
buildSteps.detail: Enzymes are improved by directed evolution (a technique recognised with the 2018 Nobel Prize in Chemistry), or a microbe is given a new metabolic pathway, so it makes the target efficiently.

buildSteps.title: Build the reactor
buildSteps.detail: Catalysts are fixed inside microfluidic channels a fraction of a millimetre wide, where temperature, pH and flow are held precisely — the approach used in continuous flow chemistry.

buildSteps.title: Add purification on a chip
buildSteps.detail: Membranes and miniature chromatography columns separate product from by-products and leftover feedstock.

buildSteps.title: Add inline analytics
buildSteps.detail: Spectrometers and flow sensors measure what is forming, so software can correct the reaction rather than run it blind.

buildSteps.title: Integrate the chassis
buildSteps.detail: Reactor, purifier, sensors, cartridge bays and waste tank are assembled into a benchtop unit with interlocks and cleaning cycles.

buildSteps.title: Validate the output
buildSteps.detail: Product purity, sterility and safety are tested batch by batch — far stricter for anything swallowed as medicine.

buildSteps.title: Load recipes
buildSteps.detail: A software library of validated synthesis routes replaces today's cookbook, and the machine runs the chosen one automatically.

prerequisites.why: microbes and enzymes already make many drugs and food ingredients, but not arbitrary molecules on demand.
compact flow systems can synthesise small batches of pharmaceuticals, showing the reactor concept works.
reactions need to run in millimetre-scale channels to be fast, safe and controllable in a kitchen.
without cheap sensors that identify molecules mid-reaction, the machine cannot confirm what it has made.

the tile's premise — reassembling base elements with high-precision lasers — requires placing individual atoms, which no laboratory can do for complex molecules and which is not how chemical synthesis works.

pathway.milestone: benchtop continuous-flow units making a handful of medicines in small batches
pathway.unlocks: proof that automated synthesis can be compact and safe.

pathway.milestone: engineered enzyme cascades making complex natural products in one vessel
pathway.unlocks: routes to molecules that today need many separate industrial steps.

pathway.milestone: cartridge appliances producing a narrow menu of pure nutrients and simple drugs at home
pathway.unlocks: a first consumer product, still far from general-purpose.
on-demand food and medicine — but this depends on atomically precise manufacturing, which remains theoretical, and even then would use prepared feedstock rather than raw elements.
